sections.text: And yet others offer as their sacrifice wealth, austerities and meditation. Monks wedded to their vows renounce their scriptural learning and even their spiritual powers.
There are some who practise control of the Vital Energy and govern the subtle forces of Prana and Apana, thereby sacrificing their Prana unto Apana, or their Apana unto Prana.
Others, controlling their diet, sacrifice their worldly life to the spiritual fire. All understand the principle of sacrifice, and by its means their sins are washed away.

We had been discussing chapter four, Gnana Karma Sannyasiyog Yoga of Renunciation of Action in Knowledge. So we had been discussing Karma Yoga in last chapter and in chapter two, Bhagavan says the Karmani Eva Adhi ka Rasthi Mafula that your right is only to act, but you have no right for your fruits of actions. So for us to understand that concept, we have to understand what action is.
So we have learnt in this chapter what action is, which then relates to what we learned about Karma Yoga. In the last chapter where we have seen that Bhagavan said Yogastha Kuro Karmani Sangam tyaktvadhananjaya. Thats the essence of Karma Yoga.
Do not expect any fruits of your action. Establish yourself in yoga and then without any attachment perform actions in this world is Karma Yoga action I must perform, but I must perform in this manner and for what I should perform action. This chapter in verse nine says Yajnar Tat Karmano anyatra Loko Yam Karma Bandanaha.
All actions other than those performed for Yajna are binding Tadartam Karma Kanthya. Therefore, perform actions for Yajna alone, Mukta Sangha Samacharaha without any attachment, with equanimity of mind. So the final advice we have seen is perform actions for Yajna.
We learnt in verse 24 then that Yajna is to understand that everything that is involved in my action is nothing but Brahman alone. There is no difference between the hunter and hunted. Its all manifestation of Brahman alone.
Say Brahmarpanam Brahma have Brahma Agna Brahma hutam. Using this metaphor of Yajna, we have learned that everything involved in this Yajna, the four things involved the instrument, the offerer, the deity and the offering itself. So these four items Bhagavan said, that is nothing but Brahman alone Brahma Eva Samadhi Nah, its only going to the Brahman alone.
This is the renunciation of action, in knowledge. Having this knowledge that all actions are performed because in and by Brahman, by the power of Brahman, Bhagawan said thats Yajna. So then next few verses we learn the 12 types of yajnas we have seen so far 10 of them from verse 25 onward.
So in verse 25 we say deva Yajna and Brahma Yajna. Deva Yajna is that when I see that all that is happening in my experience all the sense perceptions are only happening. The offerings of the sense object to the senses, the devas.
Therefore I remain detached from those experiences. Every experience I see is only happening between the sense objects and the senses. I am just a witness of whats happening that Deva Yajna.
Then we say Brahm Yajna. When I offer my limited self to my higher self. When I realized that my limited self is nothing but the expression of the higher self, it was never separated from its higher self.
As we have seen, the room space and outer space is always one and the same. Remove the room space remains where it is. My conditioned self remained where it is after my death.
It was here before my birth. So thats Brahm Yajna. That understanding firm in your mind, constantly keeping at the back of your mind in all your action.
Then sense control, thats another type of Yajna. Either control your senses so that they dont wander around or mind control. Senses may bring any information but mind does not get attached to it.
Thats the mind control. Self restraint by controlling all the senses its self restraint. So thats another Yajna we have seen. And in the last verse which we have discussed there are five Yajnas we have seen.
Dravya, Yajna, Tapa Yajna Yoga Yajna, Swadhya Yajna and Jnana Yajna. So the life of charity. Everything that I have is for charity.
Dravyajna is not just giving you one check every year during tax time. But it is something which I offer that everything I have is for the greater good. Nothing belongs to me.
What I have acquired from this world, this Prakriti, I have to give it back to the Prakriti. What I have borrowed from this Prakriti, this body, mind and intellect, they also dont belong to me. They are just lended to Me for my experiences, that type of attitude, Dravya Yajna then Tapa Yajna austerities for the self control.
When I perform certain disciplines, thats tapa Yajna then yoga Yajna, various upasanas and sadhanas. All these Yajnas are for the purification of my mind and intellect for the Antakarana Shuddhi. As a seeker of happiness, my job is only to purify my internal instrument.
Rest will happen automatically by Gods grace. The Bhagavan is partial to his Bhakta. Oh now hes praising me all the time.
It is the very nature of yourself. Just like I think that Yogi Berahur said the the more I practice, the luckier I get. My preparation made me worthy of getting that opportunity.
So here yoga is the upasana I prepare myself. Then the next one is swadhyaya. Reflecting on your own self introspection.
Who I am is this body me, this mind me, the intellect me, the accomplishments me. Thats basically is the swadhya Yajna. And then we said Gnana Yajna, Yoga of knowledge, offering your ignorance, consciously trying to get out of the veiling of this mind is Gnani Yajna.
Our learning Bhagavad Gita falls into the Gnani Yajna. The last two yajnas, the Pranayama and Pratyahara. These come from Patanjalis Yoga sutra, Ashtanga Yoga, eight parts, the Yama Niyama Asana, Pranayama Pratyaha, fourth and fifth steps of Ashtang Yoga, Pranayama Pratyah.
So verse 29 says Apane Jhuvati Pranam Pranay Apanam Tatha Apare Prana Apana Gati Ruddhwa Pranayama Prayanaha. Those who are expert, they are engaged in pranayama. They perform this pranayama in various ways.
There is not one method; there are various ways. It says Apane Jhuvati Pranam. So Apana is the outgoing breath -- and even this book says outgoing breath.
I read Bhagavan Sankaracharyas Bhashya and it says Apana is the incoming breath, which contradicts some other sources. I checked some other books and some agreed with Sankaracharyas Bhashya: Apana is incoming breath (Ap-Anaha is incoming) and Pra-Anaha is outgoing. But whichever interpretation you follow, the essential meaning of the verse does not change -- its about controlling the breath.
Lets say Apane Jhuvati Pranam -- some offer outgoing breath into the incoming breath, and Prana Apanam Tadapara -- some offer the incoming breath into the outgoing breath. In other words, two diametrically opposite practices in pranayama. Pranayama, as we have seen, is the control of all the vital energies.
But at the core of it is the control of breath, which is actually the word Svasa. If you read Patanjalis Yoga Sutra, he does not use the word Prana here. He says Svasa (incoming) and Prasvasa (outgoing).
But the overall technique is also called Pranayama. By controlling your breath, you control your pranas. All the other functions of the pranas which right now I have no control over.
So even when I am in a deep sleep, all my organs are functioning properly. My heart, my brain, my liver, my kidneys. Because the conscious mind has no control over this organ.
You can imagine if the conscious mind has to control these organs, then we will all be in lots of trouble. But conscious mind has no control over these organs or they are free of conscious mind. And therefore it functions all three states of my existence.
That waking, dream and deep sleep. But the yogis have found ways to control these functions by the conscious mind. This is called pranayama.
Their observation was that as the state of my mind change, my breathing changes. So if I can control my breathing, I may be able to control all my pranas and all my mental thoughts. So the techniques devised was to control breath.
Panditji used to say that we have finite number of breaths to take in this life. If you take faster breathing, you have a shorter life. If you have slower breathing, then you have a longer life.
So people who are calm, normally quiet, and have control over their breathing -- they live longer lives. People who are very excitable and constantly get agitated and excited, their breathing goes faster and they live shorter lives. I have no knowledge about that.
But this is what the Yoga Sutra basically says: control your breath so that you are regulating your breath. Many, many years ago when we were in Dallas, Texas, we took a course in Pranayama and Raja Yoga. One of my friends father, Mr.
Haris Raja, was a disciple of Muktananda, and he gave us pranayama training. We used to have that in early morning at 6:00. And thats a part of Raja Yoga.
So the yogas which we have seen, the pranayama, are performed in three different types of tradition. One is the Shiva Yoga. Vignana Bhairav is the book from the Kashmir Saivites.
And you see on TV this Shiva yogicant and he said that by controlling the breath, you can control all your systems. There is no need for any medication. We can control everything by controlling breathing.
Then, popularly, what we know about yoga in this country is Hatha Yoga. Hatha Yoga is basically the first three sections of Ashtanga Yoga: Yama, Niyama and Asana. We focus more on the third step, which is Asana.
But the Yoga Sutra says you should not start Pranayama until you have mastered Asanas. So Asanas are very important, and once you master the Asanas, then you do Pranayama. Many teachers I have come across say Hatha Yoga is very good, but it can also be dangerous if you are not under the guidance of a trained teacher.
Be careful, have a good teacher, then you can practice. Raja Yoga, on the other hand, is considered safer and subtler. What Pandit Ji used to teach is also Raja Yoga.
And what we learned many, many years ago, thats also Raja Yoga where basically the breathing is controlled by nine mudras. They call it remote controls. Now obviously there is no scientific study done on why that works or does it work.
But all the yogis have said that they do work. So its a apana jhuvati panam prana apanam tatha apare prana apana gatirandhwa pranayama prayanaha. Those who are expert, they engage in this pranayama.
And in Bhagavan Sankaracharyas Bhashya, I learned that the first technique of apane jhuvati pranam is called purak. We often talk about purak, Rechak and Kumbhak. Sankaracharya said these three are described here.
The first one is called purak -- when you are offering incoming breath into the outgoing. Then another is called rechak -- offering outgoing breath into incoming breath. And then pranapana gati ruddhva -- restricting the flow of air is called kumbhak.
This has to be practiced in a serial manner. So Mr. Raja used to write articles in Times of India.
Those articles were published into a book. In that he said that the goal of pranayama is our normal breathing is about 16 breaths in a minute. The goal is to reduce them to four.
So in one minute there are only four breaths. He recommends in his book -- and what he taught us back in the 80s -- 5 seconds for inhalation, then 2 seconds of inner Kumbhak (retention), then 7 seconds of exhalation. Because, he said, the air has expanded due to body temperature, so it takes longer to exhale than inhale.
That makes 14 seconds. Then you hold the breath for one second outside before taking the next breath, and you start the cycle again. That makes 15 seconds.
So there are four breaths in a minute.

These verses enumerate additional forms of yajna: Dravya Yajna (offering wealth/possessions), Tapo Yajna (austerities for self-control), Yoga Yajna (various spiritual practices and upasanas), Swadhyaya Yajna (self-study and introspection), and Jnana Yajna (the sacrifice of ignorance through knowledge). Verses 29-30 describe Pranayama - the control of vital energies through breath regulation - and Pratyahara - control of diet and withdrawal of senses. All these practitioners understand the principle of yajna, and through it their impurities are washed away (yajna-kshapita-kalmashah).
The teaching emphasizes that there is no single path that fits everyone. Human beings come in various combinations of sattva, rajas, and tamas, so numerous methods exist - scattered at the mouth of Brahman as Krishna says later. Dravya Yajna is not merely writing an annual charity check but cultivating the attitude that nothing truly belongs to you. What you borrowed from Prakriti must return to Prakriti. The discussion of Pranayama (control of breath) shows how controlling the subtle can affect the gross - by regulating breath, one can influence all pranas and mental states.
For todays practice, honestly assess which yajna suits your current temperament. If you are naturally generous, practice Dravya Yajna with awareness. If you are disciplined, try Tapo Yajna. If intellectual, focus on Swadhyaya and Jnana Yajna. If you have time, practice simple pranayama: try breathing with a rhythm of 5 seconds inhalation, 2 seconds retention, 7 seconds exhalation, 1 second pause before the next breath - this slows breathing to about 4 breaths per minute, calming the mind. Whatever practice you choose, remember the purpose: purification of the inner instrument so that knowledge may dawn. The method matters less than sincere, sustained effort aligned with your nature.
